item.title: The InSight Take: US Drug Certification: Law Enforcement or Politics?
item.dc:creator: Deborah Bonello and Jeremy McDermott
item.description:
The InSight Take: US Drug Certification: Law Enforcement or Politics?

Why did the United States remove Venezuela from its drug blacklist while Colombia and Bolivia remain on it? In this InSight Take, we unpack what Washington’s latest counternarcotics designations reveal about shifting cocaine routes, regional politics, and the Trump administration’s increasingly militarized approach to drug trafficking in Latin America.

The post The InSight Take: US Drug Certification: Law Enforcement or Politics? appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
The InSight Take: US Drug Certification: Law Enforcement or Politics?

Why did the United States remove Venezuela from its drug blacklist while Colombia and Bolivia remain on it? In this InSight Take, we unpack what Washington’s latest counternarcotics designations reveal about shifting cocaine routes, regional politics, and the Trump administration’s increasingly militarized approach to drug trafficking in Latin America.

Transcript

Deborah Bonello: [00:00:04] Last week, the White House sent Congress its annual list of countries involved in the supply of illegal drugs and those that have failed to cooperate with the United States. This process is more commonly known as a certification, and the big change this year is that Venezuela came off the list of nations that failed to cooperate. Colombia, Latin America’s biggest cocaine producer, stayed on along with Bolivia. So today we’re going to look at what is behind those decisions by the Trump administration and what they tell us about criminal dynamics in the region, as well as the implications for the removal of Venezuela. I’m Deborah Bonello, Managing Editor of InSight Crime, and I’m joined by our Co-director, Jeremy McDermott, who has lived in Colombia for 27 years, I think now.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:00:50] Covered 27 of these white House designations, so, yeah.

Deborah Bonello: [00:00:57] So tell us what exactly the presidential determination on major drug transit or major illicit drug-producing countries is, to give it its official line.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:01:09] Yeah, not so catchy, but, essentially it is where the White House looks at nations through a drug trafficking lens and any nation that plays a significant role in drug trafficking to the US can get swept up in it. It’s made up of two lists, Deb. The first list is called “the majors,” and these are the major drug transit or producing countries. And they get put on the list—it can be just geography and other factors that lend themselves to the transit or production of narcotics. And being on the list is not necessarily a reflection of the government’s efforts. It’s simply a statement of fact that these nations do play some part. There are 23 nations currently on that list; 17 of them are in our patch in Latin America. It’s the second list that’s more that’s more controversial. That’s for nations who, and I’m just going to quote directly here from the document: “who failed demonstrably over the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.” So these are the guys who are certified or decertified.

Deborah Bonello: [00:02:30] Right, so it’s the second list we really need to focus on. And there are only four nations on that list in the whole world, right? Afghanistan, Bolivia, Burma, and Colombia. Venezuela was there last year and has been since I think 2005. So its removal is pretty big news. You know, Venezuela has been pretty big news all year really, but what does it mean in practical terms to actually be on the list?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:02:59] It does have huge international and practical repercussions. It’s a public criticism of a nation by the United States and has historically had an effect on bilateral relations. But more practically, it means you lose US assistance. And American representatives at multilateral development banks, like the World Bank or the Inter-American Development Bank, they are obliged to vote against any loan requests. But there is a waiver under this system. It’s called the National Interest Waiver, which means if support to the nation in question is vital to the national interests of the United States, then support can continue uninterrupted. And three of the nations out of the four on our list have been granted that waiver. That is Burma, or Myanmar, as it’s also known, Bolivia, and Colombia. So it’s just Afghanistan that’s being sanctioned. The other three nations are still getting US aid.

Deborah Bonello: [00:04:06] So in a way, it’s more of an optic and a public sort of statement about that country than material.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:04:18] Yeah. Well, it can be material, you know, if you, if you cut aid, that’s serious. I think it’s just a chance for the US to pressure people to do, essentially, what they’re told.

Why Was Venezuela Removed From the US Drug List?

Deborah Bonello: [00:04:36] So why is Venezuela being removed from the list for the first time in over 20 years? Does it mean that the US doesn’t feel the need to apply that pressure to Venezuela anymore?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:04:47] Okay. The official reasons are, and let me quote again from President Trump’s statement: “Thanks to my administration’s arrest and removal of former illegitimate dictator and drug trafficker Nicolás Maduro and given the positive steps taken under interim President Delcy Rodríguez, I have determined that Venezuela should no longer be designated as having failed demonstrably.” Deb, President Trump has boasted that he is effectively governing Venezuela. So I think he can hardly turn around and say that it’s failing to cooperate in the fight against drugs.

SEE ALSO: Special Series: Maduro’s Arrest and Its Criminal Aftermath in Venezuela

Deborah Bonello: [00:05:28] I can see, but what about the changes that we’ve seen in Venezuela as regards the drug trade that would be required to get removed from that list, one might argue.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:05:45] Okay. Let’s look at what’s actually happened since Delcy Rodríguez took over. The first thing kind of worthy of note was the strike that killed alias Niño Guerrero, who was the head of the notorious Tren de Aragua prison gang. If you remember, he appeared, or Tren de Aragua appeared during President Trump’s campaign, accused of staging an invasion of the US, and was accused of being a drug trafficking organization, which it actually wasn’t. But that was a concrete event. I don’t think it moved the dial on drug trafficking in any sense, because as you well know from our coverage, we don’t see Tren de Aragua as a major drug trafficking organization. The issue around—the other thing that was mentioned was the Cartel of the Suns in the lead-up to the US intervention and removal of Maduro. And the Cartel of the Suns, which we’ve been covering for decades, has been managing drug trafficking through the country for quite a long time. The question is, has the removal of Nicolás Maduro done away with the Cartel of the Suns and state-buried drug trafficking in Venezuela?

Deborah Bonello: [00:07:31] Well, we are seeing Maduro being tried under a new indictment in the United States, right? Not the 2021 where he was charged with heading up the Cartel of the Suns. And I believe the Trump administration has changed its framing of what the Cartel of the Suns actually is, from defining it less as a sort of vertically structured drug cartel into more of the vision I think that our research reflects, which is that the Cartel of the Suns is an umbrella term for corruption embedded in the state that kind of aids and abets and enables the cocaine business through corruption. So my second question would be whether Rodríguez has made any moves to dismantle this network of corruption and really changed drug trafficking dynamics in the country.

SEE ALSO: The Evolution of the Cartel of the Suns

Jeremy McDermott: [00:08:27] Okay, let’s start with the 2020 indictment. As you’ve said, we’ve always had a problem with this, and we’ve written about it in the past. It portrayed Maduro and Diosdado Cabello and a couple of others as heads of a vertically integrated drug trafficking organization, which was later given the status of a “narcoterrorist organization,” Deb, which was one of the justifications, if you remember, for the US military intervention that ended up with the removal of Maduro. We’ve been investigating the Cartel of the Suns since we were founded and spent a long time investigating Maduro, and we came to the conclusion that, as you said, the Cartel of the Suns isn’t a vertically integrated drug trafficking organization. It’s a system of what we call hybrid criminal governance, and we’ve written a lot about it on the website. But the quick and dirty is that Maduro, suffering under sanctions, hyperinflation, economic mismanagement, didn’t have enough central government revenue to assure the loyalty of his generals and senior Chavista politicians. So he essentially doled out criminal fiefdoms to secure loyalty, and this means that generals or important politicians were posted to areas along the border with Colombia, or along the Caribbean coastline, where smuggling and drug trafficking corridors were present, or to Bolívar state, where all the gold deposits are. And so the deal was, they got access to criminal rents to supplement their laughable official salaries. So that was the system that Maduro presided over and we have long called that the Cartel of the Suns—even though it predates Maduro—it’s basically corruption, especially in the military, that has long been involved in the cocaine business, and then under Maduro ended up managing and regulating that business.

Deborah Bonello: [00:10:36] So before we turn to Colombia, because they are still on the list, I think it would be amiss to not mention the missile strikes that we’ve seen in the seas around Venezuela and, you know, these very kind of unprecedented missile strikes that we’ve seen happening since more than a year ago now, I believe they began at the beginning of September. Of course, that’s not the work of the Venezuelan Rodríguez administration, it’s coming from Trump, but have we seen that help sort of bring down drug trafficking activity in and around Venezuela?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:11:19] It’s had an effect on the Caribbean coast and the smuggling in the go-fast vessels that was the principal modus operandi for drug traffickers leaving the north coast of Venezuela. We’re seeing that route reopen, not using go-fast so much, but using fishing vessels and others. Perhaps the biggest change is a switch for drugs going into southern Venezuela and going across to Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, and northern Brazil. So I’m not sure if we’ve seen a massive drop necessarily in the flow of cocaine through the country, but we have seen shifts in routes. But this, again, is not to do with the Venezuelan government or any actions that it has taken. This is US policy and these strikes.

The Politics Behind the US Drug List

Deborah Bonello: [00:12:21] Okay. So let’s turn to Colombia, which was decertified last year and remains decertified, which one could argue seems a little harsh given the arrival of the conservative president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who we’ve talked about a few times already on the InSight Take, and he’s a big ally to Trump, and I think he’s kind of very firmly, you know, returning Colombia to its role as the US proxy in the region on anti-drug stuff, especially since he since he took office last month. What do you think of that decision to not take Colombia off the list because of de la Espriella’s, you know, intent. And, you know, he has already started up his anti-drug actions in Colombia, as we’ve seen.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:13:16] Well, let’s go to last year, which was the first time that Colombia had been decertified. So this is the second year. It was a huge shock in Colombia. Colombia sees itself as in the trenches in the fight against the cocaine trade, and it’s in almost daily confrontation with illegal armed actors who manage the trade. And from the Colombian perspective, all this time, the US remains the single biggest consumer of the drug. So this has caused some bitterness, especially in the security forces. But I think the original decertification, and this decertification, is more about the previous president than the country’s efforts. The statement says that it blames Colombia’s status on the “incompetence and chaos” produced by the previous left wing government of President Gustavo Petro, and he handed over office in August this year to de la Espriella.

[00:14:23] I think this is a bit personal. President Trump clearly despised Petro. Ironically, they’re very similar in many ways, which may seem odd to say, given that they’re on opposite ends of the political spectrum, but they both use social media religiously, they are both rather thin-skinned, and they both like to pick fights. And not only was the country decertified last year, but Petro was also targeted personally. He was put on the Treasury or the OFAC list, along with his wife and kids. The designation means that any US-linked assets are frozen, financial transactions can be blocked, and it’s massive stigmatization of the individual. And Trump combined this pretty extreme punishment with abuse, calling Petro a thug and accusing him of being directly involved in drug trafficking, of which there is absolutely no evidence of that, he has many failings, but involvement in drug trafficking is not one that we’ve seen, anyway. And the statement does reference the election of de la Espriella: “The people of Colombia made the courageous choice to elect a president who has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor.” So this is basically an invitation to de la Espriella that if he does do what he’s promised to do, then Colombia will come off the list next year.

Deborah Bonello: [00:16:07] But it’s not the first time that Colombia has been decertified and its president kind of named and shamed, right?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:16:15] No it’s not. Just after I arrived, President Ernesto Samper was the country’s leader and Colombia was decertified in 1996 and again in 1997. Samper was involved in a scandal where his campaign allegedly received millions of dollars from the Cali Cartel. The scandal was known as “Proceso 8,000.” The official reasons that Washington gave then for the decertification were that they hadn’t extradited the Cali Cartel leadership—and the Cali Cartel leaders were arrested in 1995 just to put that on the table—and that the country had failed to put the issue of extradition, which was constitutionally prohibited at that time, in front of Congress. So this was huge pressure on President Samper. And I think it was Madeleine Albright was then the Secretary of State, and she accused Samper of actually undermining his own police and prosecutors by working with the same criminals that they were chasing. It was about politics as well. Samper was punished. He had his US visa revoked, but he didn’t suffer anything like the sanctions that Petro is under. And one might argue that that led directly to Colombia reestablishing extradition, which it did at the end of 1997. And that’s obviously a change that’s endured. And it’s, you know, one of the central planks of the Colombia-US joint, you know, relationship as far as drug trafficking is concerned.

Deborah Bonello: [00:18:04] Right? Yeah. And President Trump’s message to Bolivia was actually pretty similar to that that he sent to Colombia this year as well. Right. He recognized the change in government, the arrival of the conservative president, Ródrigo Paz, who I think took office in November last year, unseating a socialist government. What’s your read on that?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:18:28] Yeah. It’s very similar rhetoric. The statement talks of “decades of inept socialist governments” and the opportunity to create “a new chapter” in US-Bolivian relations under President Paz. It does mention—and we covered this at the time, Deb, because it was pretty huge—the extradition of Sebastián Marset, who was—although Uruguayan, was in Bolivia and had much of his operating base in Bolivia—in March 2026, extradited to the US. But that apparently wasn’t enough, and the statement says the new government’s “not yet had sufficient time to reduce coca cultivation.” So there is the request. If President Paz can get coca crops down, then the likelihood is he’ll be off the list next year as well.

Deborah Bonello: [00:19:31] And there are other nations, from our patch here in Latin America and the Caribbean that get a mention in the president’s statement as well. What should we read into that?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:19:42] Yeah, there’s quite a few of those. Let’s list them in growing order of importance. So first of all, there’s praise for allies, you know, Argentina, Ecuador, and El Salvador: I “applaud three of America’s greatest allies in our hemisphere—Argentina, Ecuador, and El Salvador—for their leadership, resolve, and success in the fight against narcoterrorism.” The quote there. So Argentina actually isn’t even on the major’s list. So this is kind of a, you know, round of applause for their mates in the region, which is odd, that doesn’t usually happen either. Nicaragua comes in for a mention, not surprisingly: “the illegitimate Ortego-Murillo regime in Nicaragua has failed to take sufficient action against drug trafficking.” But it hasn’t been decertified. Peru got the same sort of message as Bolivia and Colombia, because Peru, of course, has a new president, Keiko Fujimori, and the statement says we “welcome the commitment of new President Keiko Fujimori” to work with the US. So again, they are listed on majors but not not decertified in any way.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:20:59] Things begin to get a little bit odd because Canada and Mexico get a rap on the knuckles, whilst recognizing Mexican President Sheinbaum’s administration for seizing greater volumes of drugs, “Mexico must take additional action against [the] narco terrorist organizations.” And of course, as we’ve discussed, Deb, the Trump administration pretty soon, upon taking office, put a series of Mexican groups on their list of foreign terrorist organizations. And Canada seems to be President Trump’s favorite punching bag at the moment, so they get a mention as well. I’m not quite sure why, but we do know that drugs come in through the Canadian border, which is obviously one of the longest borders in the world and barely policed.

SEE ALSO: US Foreign Terrorist Designations in Latin America: An Interactive Map

Jeremy McDermott: [00:21:52] The last one that’s weird is Brazil gets a mention. It’s not even on the majors list. And while it’s important in drug trafficking terms, that’s in the cocaine pipeline to Europe, Deb, as we’ve covered a great deal on the site. But the government is quoted as saying, is accused of failing to confront the designated foreign terrorist organizations, the First Capital Command and the Red Command, “which have transformed Brazil into a hub for global cocaine flows.” Now, this only happened recently, Deb, we, of course, discussed that on the website. Brazil’s cocaine doesn’t go to the United States, so I’m not sure why this, you know, this is not a direct threat to the United States, so one wonders why it’s being mentioned in this, except, of course, that President Lula, the president of Brazil, has openly defied President Trump, pushed back on tariffs, squeezed on rare earth minerals, and basically refused to be to be bullied. And so one wonders again, if this is a wee bit personal.

Deborah Bonello: [00:23:10] I mean, what I’m hearing is the whole process is as much about politics as it is about drug trafficking. And has that always been the case, or is this something that has come into focus under Donald Trump? And of course, we should mention this is all taking place on the stage of the Shield of the Americas alliance that’s being slowly built throughout the region, which of course, is very much an initiative from Donald Trump.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:23:40] I think it’s always been somewhat about politics, Deb. It has been an annual excuse for Washington to pressure political leaders to do what the US wants of them in terms of the fight against drugs. But I do think under President Trump, it has become even more political. You know, if you look at this year’s one, this is about, hey, look at my mates, they’re all doing really well, you know, love ’em. And that, you know, it’s the left wing and socialist governments that have really made a bit of a hash of things, and don’t worry, now that, you know, Colombia, and Peru, and Bolivia have right-leaning leaders, we’re expecting, you know, great things, and Colombia and Bolivia will hopefully soon get off the list. So, it is framed in a much more political way, and I think it is being used by President Trump to push his agenda, which is different, you know, this military-first agenda that we’re seeing, the Shield of the Americas, is something different from before. But previous presidents have used this tool to pressure governments ever since the process began. So you know, I would say that politics has always been perhaps a fairly significant part of this.

The Future of US Drug Policy in Latin America

Deborah Bonello: [00:25:09] So what do you think the takeaways should be for our audience with respect to this year’s statement? And what do you think we can expect to see this time next year?

Jeremy McDermott: [00:25:19] Well, one, I think Colombia will come off the list. I think that Bolivia, if President Paz gets the message loud and clear and manages to reduce, do some coca eradication, will perhaps get off the list. And like Venezuela, Bolivia has been on the list for a long time—I think since 2008, or 18 years. And the Venezuela situation I don’t think is going to change, obviously. The United States is still very much, has very strong influence over Delcy Rodríguez, and it really can’t be decertified because, you know, the US has such a strong role in Venezuela’s government at the moment. But I think if we take a step back and go, okay, what are the drug trafficking dynamics? And how much are they going to change over the coming months, or over the next 12 months, before the next series of announcements? This is all built around the Shield of the Americas and the militarized approach, and those who sign up to it—and, you know, most of the region now have, apart from, say, Mexico and Brazil—then they will be rewarded, in terms of not being named and shamed by Washington.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:26:58] The question we have to ask ourselves, as we divorce ourselves from the politics and the geopolitics in the region, is this going to move the dial on drug trafficking in the region? And as we discussed in the previous InSight Take, we are worried about the limitations of a purely military-only approach, and next year will be the acid test, to be honest. And if there—there have been no real changes so far for the—if we look at the last 18 months of the Trump administration, we have seen a shift in routes and modus operandi, mainly due to the strikes on the go-fast boats. The price of cocaine in the United States is perhaps lower than it’s ever been. The flow to Europe and the global development of the trade of cocaine trade is continuing apace. So, so far we haven’t seen any major changes to the drug industry in the Western Hemisphere.

Deborah Bonello: [00:28:06] Yeah. And I’d be interested too, Jerry, I don’t know what you think—one of the things we talked about in past InSight Takes about the Shield of the Americas, which, of course, does intertwine with certification or decertification, is whether we’re going to see any more specifics on what exactly that alliance is going to do. What are the requirements of the member governments? Does it include any extra aid from the US? Do you think we might see more details emerge there by this time next year.

Jeremy McDermott: [00:28:37] Hopefully. I, you know, I wouldn’t dare to speculate on what’s going on in the White House around this. So yeah, we are waiting with bated breath, aren’t we, Deb? And of course, as soon as any announcements are made, we will no doubt be talking again and trying to pick them apart and put them into the context of an historical framework that we do when we analyze everything in the region.

Deborah Bonello: [00:29:06] We will. That seems like a good place to end. Jerry, thanks for thanks for speaking to me today. You’ve just watched the InSight Take, to those at home, our weekly video analysis of the biggest organized crime stories in the region. Of course, we have long-running coverage and investigations of Venezuela’s cocaine economy, as well as all of its criminal groups, including the ELN from Colombia, which has expanded, of course, across the border into Venezuela and the Cartel of the Suns. You can find all of that and more at insightcrime.org. And you can find the InSight Take on our website, as well as on YouTube and Spotify. And of course, if there’s a story you’d like us to take apart, then please reach out to me at flagship@insightcrime.org. We’ll be back next week. Bye for now.

item.content:encoded:
On The Radar | US Drops Venezuela From Its Drugs Blacklist. Colombia Could Be Next

Is Venezuela no longer a major drug transit point?

What does the US win from Alex Saab’s cooperation—and what does Venezuela lose?

How do criminal groups prey on the people defending Latin America’s land and resources?

Which is the latest country to sign on to Trump’s Shield of the Americas?

This week’s top three organized crime stories in On the Radar.

1: White House Removes Venezuela from Drug List, May Also Drop Colombia

The White House removed Venezuela from its list of major drug transit or major illicit drug producing countries for fiscal year 2027. US President Donald Trump said that given the “positive steps taken under interim President Delcy Rodríguez,” his administration determined “Venezuela should no longer be designated as having failed demonstrably to fulfill its drug control commitments.”

The decision is a reward for the government of Rodríguez, but InSight Crime’s on-the-ground investigations have found that a large share of the cocaine produced in South America moves through Venezuela, where transport networks have long taken advantage of the country’s long, porous border with Colombia and extensive coastline. Cocaine shipments are then moved through Caribbean nations like Trinidad and Tobago before reaching consumers in the United States and Europe.

Trump also said that “Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in ‌the ⁠hemisphere” with the arrival of Aberlardo de la Espriella as president.

2: Maduro’s Frontman Pleads Guilty in Miami

Alex Saab, the Colombian-born businessman, the alleged financial frontman of former Venezuela President Nicolás Maduro, pleaded guilty to a single count of conspiracy to launder money in a Miami court on Tuesday. He admitted to organizing bribes to Venezuelan officials so companies he secretly controlled could win contracts under the state-funded food and medicine program, and agreed to forfeit $195 million and cooperate with continuing federal investigations. Saab was deported to the United States in May by interim President Delcy Rodríguez, having been pardoned by the Biden administration and returned to Caracas less than three years earlier. 

AP reported that US officials could seek Saab’s testimony against Maduro, who was arrested in a US military operation in Caracas on January 3 and is awaiting trial in New York on narco-terrorism, cocaine trafficking, and weapons charges. Our special series on Maduro’s arrest covers how criminal power is shifting in Venezuela post-Maduro, Rodríguez’s government has delivered purges, mining raids, and Saab’s deportation, as well as conducted joint operations with the US against the Claritas Sindicato and Tren de Aragua founder Héctor Guerrero Flores, alias “Niño Guerrero,” who was killed in a US strike in June. But, the country’s deeply embedded hybrid criminal architecture remains mostly intact. 

3: Organized Crime Is the Leading Suspect in Killings of Land Defenders

Organized crime or contract killers were suspected in more than a third of all cases of the killing of land and environmental defenders worldwide, making criminal actors the most frequently implicated perpetrators. At least 105 defenders—85 percent of the global total—were killed in Latin America in 2025, according to Global Witness, and Colombia was the deadliest country in the region.

Criminal groups prey  on land defenders in two ways. The first is direct: our GameChangers 2025 analysis of environmental crime in the Amazon traced how armed groups have moved into unauthorized gold mining, logging, and land grabbing, and how anyone documenting or protesting that expansion becomes a target. The second is slower and harder to count: our investigation Corruption Kills showed how extractive projects  in Honduras captured the permitting, prosecutorial, and judicial machinery that was supposed to protect communities so that killings go uninvestigated and threats continue. 

4: The Shield of the Americas Grows

Peru is the latest country in the region to sign up for the Shield of the Americas regional security coalition, President Keiko Fujimori announced in Lima at the end of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s tour of Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. Days later, Chilean President José Antonio Kast told Radio Agricultura that his country would remain an observer for now. Meanwhile, soldiers from Peru, the United States, Argentina, and Chile spent the week training together near Tarapoto in the Peruvian Amazon under Southern Vanguard 2026, an exercise run by US Army South.

The Shield of the Americas coalition keeps adding members, but as InSight Crime’s co-director Jeremy McDermott and managing editor Deborah Bonello argue in this InSight Take, months after its founding it still has no approved operational plan, no defined targets beyond drug trafficking and “narco-terrorism,” and no clear obligations for the governments signing up.

Delcy Rodríguez’s silent dismantling of a subsidized food program shutters a scheme that epitomized the intersection of organized crime and the Venezuelan state. item.content:encoded:
How a Food Program Fueled Venezuela’s Organized Crime

Delcy Rodríguez’s silent dismantling of a subsidized food program, the CLAP (Comités Locales de Abastecimiento y Producción), shutters a scheme that epitomized the intersection of organized crime and the Venezuelan state.

The CLAP program was established in 2016 under President Nicolás Maduro during a severe economic crisis and period of food scarcity. Over the following decade, boxes of basic goods such as beans, pasta, and oil were distributed throughout the country. According to local media and both CLAP recipients and providers interviewed by InSight Crime, the boxes began arriving with increasing delays in August of 2025, until stopping altogether by early 2026. 

SEE ALSO: How Criminals Take Advantage of Venezuela’s Food Aid System

While the government has yet to issue any formal notice about the program’s end, the Rodríguez administration has already started to implement new food assistance initiatives, such as grocery stores selling at discounted prices.

The apparent discontinuation of the food subsidy program marks the end of an era in which hunger was exploited and instrumentalized by both corruption networks within the state and allied and hybrid criminal groups that strengthened their power through the food boxes they obtained.

CLAP and the Hybrid Criminal State

While CLAP provided food to an impoverished populace, it also became both a criminal rent and a tool for social control, making it an important component of the criminal-hybrid state model developed under the Maduro administration. 

The CLAP program was used by Chavista officials and politically connected businessmen for both illicit self-enrichment and complex money laundering schemes. One of the most emblematic of these figures is Alex Saab, a Colombian businessman alleged to be a frontman for Maduro, who has been charged in the United States with money laundering related to the CLAP program.

Under Saab and his business partner, Alvaro Enrique Pulido Vargas, the CLAP program purchased food and assembled packages in foreign countries, such as Mexico, before importing the finished boxes to Venezuela, according to the US Department of the Treasury. Venezuelan state-owned companies allegedly bought the boxes at hyperinflated prices, to the benefit of Saab, Pulido, and others involved. The funds used to purchase these boxes were also allegedly used to carry out convoluted bribery and kickback schemes throughout the country. The food itself was often inedible and frequently found to contain different ingredients than listed, according to a series of investigations by investigative outlet Armando.info. 

The Maduro regime also allowed CLAP boxes to be distributed by allied criminal groups, both for the benefit of the state and the criminal groups themselves.

The National Liberation Army (Ejército de Liberación Nacional – ELN), a guerrilla group active in Colombia and Venezuela, used the CLAP program as a political tool. In 2018, the Venezuelan non-governmental organization Fundación Redes reported that the ELN controlled distribution of CLAP boxes in municipalities bordering Colombia and stuck labels with pro-ELN messages on the boxes before delivering them.

Criminal gangs, such as Carlos Capa and Tren de Aragua, were also allowed to distribute the CLAP boxes to generate profit. According to Transparencia Venezuela, a Venezuelan NGO operating in exile, Tren de Aragua controlled at least 66 CLAP localities through its Somos al Barrio JK Foundation. Rather than distributing boxes at subsidized prices, the criminal groups would demand higher payments.

SEE ALSO: Hybrid Governance and the Criminal Fiefdoms of Tren de Aragua

Colectivos, pro-regime armed groups, used CLAP boxes for both criminal and political ends. These groups used the CLAP for pro-Chavista voter manipulation, purposefully positioning food distribution infrastructure at “puntos rojos”—stations for Venezuelans to renew their “Carnet de la Patria” cards used to access CLAP boxes—alongside polling stations during elections. In this way, the Maduro regime outsourced political coercion.

Although the boxes at one point were sources of both income and propaganda for these groups, their disappearance is unlikely to noticeably disrupt their operations. Many of the gangs that previously distributed the boxes have since been dismantled or severely weakened by the government. Additionally, the ELN’s diversified revenue streams, which include illegal gold mining, drug trafficking, and extortion, mean they aren’t reliant on income from the CLAP. The colectivos, which have traditionally been heavily reliant on ever-dwindling state resources, are most likely to be affected by the end of this program. The end of the CLAP may increase their growing reliance on extortion and other criminal economies to make up for the shortfall in income.

The post How a Food Program Fueled Venezuela’s Organized Crime appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.title: The US Anti-Drug Missile Strikes Are Back. But Are They Working?
item.dc:creator: Sean Doherty
item.description:
The US Anti-Drug Missile Strikes Are Back. But Are They Working?

The United States launched new reported strikes on vessels suspected of transporting drugs in late August—the first bombings after a two-month hiatus. The latest missile strikes suggest the Trump administration is sticking with a tactic that evidence suggests has failed to curb drug trafficking.

The post The US Anti-Drug Missile Strikes Are Back. But Are They Working? appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
The US Anti-Drug Missile Strikes Are Back. But Are They Working?

The United States launched new strikes on vessels suspected of transporting drugs in late August—the first attacks after a two-month hiatus. The latest missile strikes suggest the Trump administration is sticking with a tactic that evidence suggests has so far failed to curb drug trafficking.

US President Trump has said that maritime drug trafficking to the United States dropped dramatically since the strikes began in September 2025, even claiming it had fallen 98% by January. But US Border Patrol (USBP) and Office of Field Operations (OFO) drug seizures tell a different story. 

Drug seizures can operate as a proxy, albeit a far-from-perfect one, for the amount of drugs passing through an area. Seizures of cocaine, the drug most likely to be aboard the targeted vessels, at or between ports of entry to the United States fell by less than 3% in the 11 months following the beginning of the strikes when compared with the same period the year prior. A supply shortage also typically pushes the prices of a drug up, but cocaine prices in the United States have also remained largely stable, further challenging the notion that supply has been reduced.

SEE ALSO: The InSight Take: The Shield of the Americas Grows, But Does it Have a Strategy?

There is evidence that strikes have disrupted specific routes forcing smugglers to adopt alternate routes or methods, but they have not substantially reduced drug trafficking.

Some traffickers initially abandoned coastal drug trafficking export points in Venezuela following the strikes, and trafficking to nearby islands such as Aruba, Curaçao, and Trinidad all but froze for a time, according to InSight Crime investigations. But seizures near Aruba in June and July show that traffickers are continuing to use these routes. Alternatives have also sprung up, with a reported increase in drug flights from Venezuela into Guyana after the strikes began in the Caribbean Sea near Venezuela. 

Recent drug confiscations in or near Guyana’s neighbor Suriname suggest that routes departing these countries could be becoming more fixed. Drug traffickers are also using larger boats and sticking closer to coastlines to reduce the likelihood of potential attacks, according to a Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) assessment the Washington Post reviewed.

SEE ALSO: Timeline of US Strikes Against Alleged Drug Boats

The most recent strikes indicate that the controversial campaign is set to continue, regardless of its questionable impact.

Lethal strikes on August 23 and 25 were followed by a joint operation with Ecuador on August 28. US Marines and sailors sank what the US military described as a floating refueling station that the Ecuadorian crime group the Choneros used for vessels transporting drugs. Unlike the previously reported strikes at sea, this time US forces removed those aboard before destroying the vessel.

US authorities have failed to provide evidence of their assertion that the boats and people targeted in strikes, which have killed 227 people since September 2025, were trafficking drugs. The process used in planning the strikes remains relatively opaque, but US Senator Tim Kaine revealed in June that evidence of drugs aboard a vessel is not one of the three criteria used to determine which vessels to attack. The intelligence behind the strikes has been questioned, with a Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA) report identifying a lack of rigor in identifying those aboard or their alleged affiliation to drug trafficking organizations. 

SEE ALSO: US Foreign Terrorist Designations in Latin America: An Interactive Map

The strikes are part of a wider regional anti-drug push from the United States. The US Coast Guard continues making large seizures, and the Treasury has aggressively sanctioned alleged drug traffickers. The State Department has designated 20 criminal groups in the region as Foreign Terrorist Organizations since last year. The latest missile strikes at sea came a few weeks after the latest meeting of the US-led military initiative, the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C), also known as the Shield of the Americas alliance, an initiative pushed by the Trump government as part of calls for a more militarized anti-drug strategy across the region.

Correction: A previous version of this article claimed that DEA analysts had told the Washington Post that drug traffickers are using larger boats and sticking closer to coastlines to reduce the likelihood of potential attacks. This information references a DEA assessment the Washington Post reviewed.

The post The US Anti-Drug Missile Strikes Are Back. But Are They Working? appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.dc:creator: Daniel Reyes
item.description:
Why Organized Crime in Venezuela Won’t Die Without Maduro

Nicolás Maduro has been removed. So why hasn’t Venezuela’s organized crime problem disappeared with him? Because the system was never built around one person.

The post Why Organized Crime in Venezuela Won’t Die Without Maduro appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
Why Organized Crime in Venezuela Won’t Die Without Maduro

Nicolás Maduro has been removed. So why hasn’t Venezuela’s organized crime problem disappeared with him? Because the system was never built around one person.

Over decades, criminal economies became embedded in Venezuela’s political institutions, security forces, and territory. Drug trafficking networks, illegal mining groups, prison gangs, guerrillas, and state officials became interconnected parts of what InSight Crime calls a “hybrid state.”

Even if the faces at the top of the regime have changed, the machinery underneath is far harder to dismantle.

Our latest video explains how organized crime evolved in Venezuela, and what needs to happen to truly weaken the country’s criminal networks and economies.

The post Why Organized Crime in Venezuela Won’t Die Without Maduro appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.title: National Liberation Army (ELN)
item.dc:creator: InSight Crime
item.description:
National Liberation Army (ELN)

The National Liberation Army (Ejército de Liberación Nacional – ELN) is Colombia’s last true insurgency and one of Latin America’s most powerful criminal organizations.

The post National Liberation Army (ELN) appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
National Liberation Army (ELN)

The National Liberation Army (Ejército de Liberación Nacional – ELN) is Colombia’s last remaining insurgent group and one of the most powerful criminal organizations in Latin America. Its expansion and consolidation in Venezuela over the past decade have progressively transformed it into a binational structure.

SEE ALSO: ELN in Venezuela

Originally formed as a Marxist-Leninist guerrilla group influenced by the Cuban Revolution, the ELN focused on extortion, kidnappings, and attacks on oil infrastructure in its early years. Although it distanced itself from drug trafficking for decades, several of its structures now control key cocaine enclaves in Colombia.

Its growing involvement in criminal economies such as drug trafficking and illegal mining has led to the criminalization of its fronts and a drift away from political work, contributing to the failure of multiple peace negotiation attempts. While in Colombia it operates as a rebel group and is pursued by security forces, in Venezuela it acts more like a paramilitary army with government backing.

Recent ELN News

August 11, 2026 — De la Espriella’s Government Bombs ELN Camp in Catatumbo

Colombia’s military bombed a camp belonging to the ELN’s Northeastern War Front in a rural area between San Calixto and Tibú, Norte de Santander, in the first airstrike by the government of Abelardo de la Espriella. The operation followed clashes between special forces and members of the criminal group. Preliminary reports from the authorities say that two alleged ELN members were killed and several structures in the camp were destroyed. Weapons, drones, and explosives were also seized.

Table of contents

  • Recent ELN News
  • What’s the Story of the ELN?
  • Who Are The ELN’s Leaders?
  • Where Does the ELN Operate?
  • Who Are the ELN’s Allies and Enemies?
  • What is the Future of the ELN?

What’s the Story of the ELN?

The ELN emerged in the 1960s, as Colombia was recovering from a bloody period of political violence, and a range of social and student movements were being shaped by the Cold War and the Cuban Revolution.

The most radical segments of these movements came together in July 1964 to form the nucleus of the guerrilla group. A small armed insurgency began training in San Vicente de Chucurí, a town in eastern Colombia in the department of Santander, less than 400 kilometers from the Venezuelan border.

On January 7, 1965, the group carried out its first major attack, the seizure of Simacota, a small municipality in Santander. There, it formally announced its creation under the leadership of Fabio Vásquez Castaño, a student leader who drew on the political and military training he received in Cuba to establish a guerrilla movement in Colombia.

From the outset, the ELN was a highly ideological organization, combining Marxist-Leninist doctrine with liberation theology, a Catholic religious movement inspired by struggles against inequality in Latin America. Some of the ELN’s early members had direct ties to the Catholic Church.

The group, however, suffered a series of military defeats following the Simacota attack that left it on the brink of annihilation. A military offensive in 1973, known as “Operation Anorí,” wiped out much of the group and weakened its command structure. This forced the guerrillas to retreat toward the Venezuelan border, specifically to the department of Arauca, to reorganize. It also pushed the group into its first peace talks with the Colombian government, which began in 1975.

After Operation Anorí, Manuel Pérez, a Spanish priest known by the alias “El Cura,” along with Nicolás Rodríguez Bautista, alias “Gabino,” took control of the ELN and played a decisive role in its military and financial restructuring. Both oversaw the group’s expansion into the departments of Casanare and Boyacá, near the Venezuelan border, as well as Nariño and Putumayo in southern Colombia.

During the 1990s, the ELN’s violent reputation grew, even as it took part in failed peace negotiations in 1994 and 1998.

In 1999, the ELN kidnapped 190 people from a church in the city of Cali, in western Colombia, in what remains the largest kidnapping in the country’s history. The group also hijacked a commercial airplane, forcing it to land in a remote area in southern Bolívar department and holding its passengers hostage.

Mounting pressure from Colombian security forces, along with attacks by other non-state armed groups such as the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia – AUC) and the guerrillas of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia – FARC), compelled the ELN to abandon some territories and expand its presence in Venezuela. By the late 1990s, the group had found favor with then-Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez, an outspoken ally of both the ELN and the FARC.

These shifts also led ELN commanders to rethink their financial, military, and political strategies across Colombia. Several ELN fronts moved into new criminal economies, including drug trafficking and illegal mining.

Although the ELN initially opposed direct involvement in drug trafficking, the transformation of Colombia’s armed conflict and the weakening of the guerrilla pushed it to seek new sources of financing. Some structures levied taxes on farmers, coca growers, and traffickers, while others became directly involved in drug production and international trafficking, particularly along the border between Colombia’s Norte de Santander department and Venezuela’s Zulia state.

The ELN took part in another round of failed peace talks with the Colombian government between 2005 and 2007, which collapsed due to disagreements between the parties and the deterioration of Colombia’s relationship with Venezuela, which was acting as a facilitator.

Seven years later, in 2014, the ELN resumed peace negotiations with the government of President Juan Manuel Santos, running parallel to the peace process with the FARC (2012–2016). Talks with the ELN continued briefly under Santos’ successor, Iván Duque, but collapsed in 2019 after the guerrillas attacked a police academy in Bogotá.

Following the demobilization of the FARC, the ELN moved to fill the territorial vacuums left by its former rival. The group expanded its involvement in criminal economies in both Colombia and Venezuela, aided by the permissive stance of Nicolás Maduro, Chávez’s successor.

The ELN consolidated its presence along the Colombia–Venezuela border, controlling major clandestine crossings used for smuggling and migrant trafficking. It also deepened its role in illegal mining, with the acquiescence of military and political sectors loyal to Maduro, in Venezuela’s Bolívar state.

As Venezuela became increasingly central to the Colombian insurgency, senior commanders decided to relocate across the border.

The ELN began operating as a binational guerrilla force. In Colombia, it remains focused on territorial control, locked in constant clashes with law enforcement, and undergoing a criminalization of its fronts, which, while still maintaining an ideological struggle, are increasingly tied to the control of illicit economies. In Venezuela, the ELN’s ideological affinities and strategic alliances with the government have pushed it to function as a paramilitary group, coordinating operations with security forces, interfering in elections, and helping the government control key areas.

In 2022, a strengthened ELN resumed peace talks with Colombia’s new president, Gustavo Petro, with Venezuela serving as a guarantor. The negotiations have seen major ups and downs, but in May 2024 the parties agreed on the first item on the peace agenda, marking the most significant advance of any peace talks with the ELN.

The process, however, faced serious obstacles. Among them were the insurgent leadership’s refusal to abandon kidnapping as a source of financing and its continued use of violence against civilians. As a result, negotiations with the ELN under Petro’s government became mired in rhetoric and failed to produce tangible changes on the ground.

Internal divisions within the armed group further complicated matters. In May 2024, the Comuneros del Sur, a substructure of the Southwestern War Front, broke away from the ELN to form a dissident faction that announced its intention to pursue a separate peace process with the Colombian government.

Peace efforts ultimately collapsed when the insurgency launched a military offensive in the Catatumbo region in January 2025, aiming to expel the 33rd Front of FARC dissidents and seize control of another strategic area along the binational border with Venezuela.

Who Are The ELN’s Leaders?

The ELN has a confederated structure in which its war fronts retain a degree of operational and financial autonomy. Political decisions are handled by a leadership body known as the Central Command (Comando Central – COCE), made up of five commanders responsible for the group’s most important decisions.

Below the COCE sits the National Directorate (Dirección Nacional – DINAL), a body composed of 23 representatives elected by the ELN’s eight war fronts. Each front is, in turn, led by a commander, a political chief, and a military chief. According to official figures from 2025, the ELN has approximately 6,300 members, including combatants and support networks or militia members, around 20% of whom are based in Venezuela.

Eliécer Erlinto Chamorro, alias “Antonio García,” serves as the guerrilla group’s commander-in-chief. He is joined on the COCE by Israel Ramírez Pineda, alias “Pablo Beltrán,” the political commander and chief negotiator; Rafael Sierra, alias “Ramiro Vargas,” in charge of international affairs; Jaime Galvis Rivera, alias “Ariel,” the financial commander; and Aníbal Giraldo, alias “Pablito,” who oversees military strategy.

Where Does the ELN Operate?

The ELN operates in at least 184 municipalities across 19 departments in Colombia and in eight of Venezuela’s 24 states, according to intelligence reports.

The Northeastern War Front “Manuel Pérez Martínez” (Frente de Guerra Nororiental – FGNO) exerts influence in the Colombian departments of Norte de Santander and Cesar, and in Venezuela’s Zulia state. It is currently led by Leonel Salazar Roa, alias “Gonzalo Satélite.”

The Northern War Front (Frente de Guerra Norte – FGN) operates in the Colombian departments of La Guajira, Cesar, Magdalena, and Atlántico, as well as in the Venezuelan states of Zulia and Táchira. It is currently led by a commander known by the alias “El Poeta.”

The Eastern War Front “Manuel Vásquez Castaño” (Frente de Guerra Oriental – FGO) has influence in the Colombian departments of Arauca, Boyacá, Vichada, Guainía, and Casanare, and in the Venezuelan states of Apure, Táchira, and Amazonas. Alias “Pablito” commanded the front until 2016 and remains one of its most influential figures.

The Jesús Darío Ramírez Castro War Front (Frente de Guerra Jesús Darío Ramírez Castro – FGJDR) operates in the department of Antioquia and southern Bolívar. The front was led by Gustavo Wilfredo Vásquez Castrillón, alias “Pirry,” until his death in early 2022.

The Western War Front “Omar Gómez” (Frente de Guerra Occidental – FGO) has influence in the departments of Chocó and Risaralda. It was led by Ogli Ángel Padilla Romero, alias “Fabián,” until his death in 2021, and is currently commanded by Emilce Oviedo Sierra, alias “Martha” or “La Abuela.”

Some fronts lack a clearly defined commander, including the Southwestern War Front “Carlos Alberto Troches Zuleta” (Frente de Guerra Suroccidental – FGSO), which operates in the departments of Nariño and Cauca, and the Central War Front (Frente de Guerra Central – FGC), with influence in Tolima, Risaralda, and Antioquia.

The National Urban War Front (Frente de Guerra Urbano Nacional – FGUN) is believed to maintain cells in Colombia’s main cities, including Medellín, Barranquilla, Bogotá, and Cali. However, its activities have been less visible than those of other fronts. The alleged commander of the FGUN is Jaime Galvis Rivera, alias “Ariel” or “Lorenzo Alcantruz.”

In Venezuela, the states with the ELN’s strongest presence are Zulia, Táchira, Apure, and Amazonas. In these areas, the guerrillas have established themselves in border municipalities that allow them to control criminal economies and ensure mobility between Colombia and Venezuela.

The ELN has also expanded into central and eastern Venezuelan states such as Bolívar, Anzoátegui, and Guárico.

Who Are the ELN’s Allies and Enemies?

The ELN has faced a wide range of adversaries, including paramilitary groups, armed insurgencies, and Venezuelan criminal gangs.

One of the ELN’s main enemies in Colombia is the Gaitanist Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (Autodefensas Gaitanistas de Colombia – AGC), also known as the Gulf Clan. In Antioquia and Chocó, the two groups have been locked in a territorial dispute since 2018 over control of key areas for drug trafficking and illegal mining, with the AGC successfully pushing into zones that were traditionally under ELN control.

Along the Pacific coast, in Valle del Cauca, Cauca, and Nariño, the ELN competes with several dissident factions of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia aligned with the Central General Staff (Estado Mayor Central – EMC) for control of coca production, drug trafficking routes, mining revenues, and other key criminal economies. To counter the EMC — which has more fighters and broader territorial reach — the ELN forged an alliance with the Second Marquetalia (Segunda Marquetalia), another FARC dissident faction, in southwestern Colombia.

Along the Colombia–Venezuela border, particularly in the Arauca–Apure corridor, the ELN previously clashed with the 10th Front of FARC dissidents aligned with the EMC. By 2019, reports indicated that both groups had reached non-aggression agreements in the departments of Arauca, Boyacá, and Casanare. However, in 2022, the 10th Front and the ELN’s Domingo Laín Front began fighting in Arauca and Apure, in a conflict that also involved Venezuelan security forces and elements of another FARC dissident faction, the Second Marquetalia.

Since 2018, the Second Marquetalia had maintained agreements with the ELN in Venezuela’s Apure and Amazonas states aimed at defining territorial boundaries and dividing criminal revenues. That alliance, however, appears to have fractured after the ELN ambushed and killed José Manuel Sierra Sabogal, alias “Zarco Aldinever,” the dissident faction’s second-in-command, in August 2025.

In Norte de Santander and Cesar — two Colombian departments along the border with Venezuela — the ELN displaced the Popular Liberation Army (Ejército Popular de Liberación – EPL) and became one of the most powerful armed actors in the area. In that same region, the guerrillas reached a non-aggression pact with the 33rd Front of FARC dissidents, which collapsed in January 2026 and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis. In the aftermath, the ELN emerged as the dominant force in the region.

In Venezuela, meanwhile, the ELN’s most significant alliances are with segments of the country’s authorities, allowing the group to operate with relative freedom. This relationship is most evident in states along the Colombian border, where the guerrillas maintain ties with members of the security forces and political authorities.

What is the Future of the ELN?

The ELN’s gradual dominance along the Colombia–Venezuela border has given it access to significant criminal revenues, consolidating its position as one of the region’s leading criminal groups and one of the most serious security threats. Strategic control of the border has also allowed the ELN to amass resources that it can funnel to other fronts across Colombia, ensuring the continuity of its operations and expanding its territorial influence.

Beyond its rear base in Venezuela, the group’s binational nature is rooted in its close ties to political sectors and security forces forged during the regime of Nicolás Maduro, which could be disrupted following Maduro’s arrest and transfer to the United States in January 2025 to stand trial in a federal court on drug trafficking-related charges.

The ELN has once again derailed the prospects for a peace agreement with the Colombian government. With its presence firmly entrenched in Venezuela, increased income from illicit economies, and a consolidated binational structure, disarming the organization stands out as one of the central challenges facing future governments in Colombia.

The post National Liberation Army (ELN) appeared first on InSight Crime.

item.title: Mapping Latin America’s Megaprisons
item.dc:creator: Liza Schmidt
item.description:
Mapping Latin America’s Megaprisons

In the three years since President of El Salvador Nayib Bukele opened his famous Terrorism Confinement Center, leaders around Latin America have attempted to follow in his footsteps in hopes of replicating El Salvador’s success in repressing gangs. Yet many of these initiatives function more as political signaling than substantive policy changes.  Here, InSight Crime analyzes the region’s proposals for new megaprisons.

The post Mapping Latin America’s Megaprisons appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
Mapping Latin America’s Megaprisons

In the three years since President of El Salvador Nayib Bukele opened his famous Terrorism Confinement Center (Centro de Confinamiento de Terrorismo – CECOT), leaders around Latin America have attempted to follow in his footsteps in hopes of replicating El Salvador’s success in repressing gangs. 

CECOT is one of the cornerstones of Bukele’s mano dura (iron fist) crackdown on organized crime in El Salvador. It is located in Tecoluca, about 70 kilometers east of San Salvador, and boasts a capacity of 40,000 prisoners.

Built in just seven months, the prison opened in February 2023 to much hype—dramatic videos showing tattooed and shirtless prisoners rushing into massive cell blocks, heavily armed guards patrolling row upon row of men seated in tight lines with their heads bowed, sweeping drone footage of the prison’s expansive grounds—all highly polished and widely promoted on social media by the Bukele government. Between CECOT and other facilities, Bukele’s government has imprisoned nearly 2% of the country’s population.

Bukele’s crackdown began in March 2022, after a gang massacre left 86 dead. In response, Bukele implemented a state of emergency, suspending many constitutional rights and loosening rules on making arrests in the name of fighting organized crime. This state of emergency, which has since been renewed for 52 consecutive months, led to the arrest of tens of thousands of suspected gang members and collaborators, as well as widespread reports of human rights abuses ranging from arbitrary arrests to torture. 

SEE ALSO: How El Salvador’s (Perpetual) State of Emergency: How Bukele’s Government Overpowered Gangs

Bukele’s relentless efforts have successfully weakened the Mara Salvatrucha (MS13) and Barrio 18 gangs that once terrorized El Salvador, after decades of failed attempts by other governments. 

Leaders throughout Latin America are attempting to mimic Bukele’s approach, including building their own “megaprisons.” During her term as president of Honduras, Xiomara Castro announced plans for a megaprison that would hold 20,000. Rodrigo Chaves in Costa Rica and Dina Boluarte in Peru announced similar plans during their tenures as president, and under Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Raúl Mulino in Panama, and Bernardo Arévalo in Guatemala, construction on such facilities has begun. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said during his campaign that he plans to build 10 new megaprisons during his mandate. Yet many of these initiatives function more as political signaling than substantive policy changes. 

Below, InSight Crime analyzes the region’s proposals for new megaprisons.

Megaprisons Around the Region

Since the opening of CECOT in 2023, there have been 16 megaprisons proposed in 10 countries around the region.

Several of these prisons have not made it past the proposal phase or were halted in early construction stages. The plans for a prison on Honduras’ Swan Islands in the Caribbean were quashed on environmental protection grounds. A proposal for a facility in Ananea, Puno, Peru, that would hold 30,000 prisoners was never even approved. While others in Panama, Ecuador, and Peru have been approved, construction has not yet begun. 

Ecuador’s Noboa has been a particularly strong supporter of the mano dura approach. Like Bukele, Noboa declared an internal armed conflict against the country’s criminal groups in January 2024 after gang violence in Ecuador exploded in response to increased cocaine flows. Since then, he has proposed the construction of several prisons. “For all the Bukele lovers, this prison will be exactly the same,” he said when announcing his prison plans.

One is already operational: the Santa Elena No. 1 Detention Center, also known as “El Encuentro,” in Santa Elena province in western Ecuador. Another facility for 15,000 prisoners was announced in November 2025, though further details have not yet been shared. 

The Minga Guazú Social Reintegration Center in Alto Paraná, Paraguay, is the other operational megaprison in the region, though it is far smaller than CECOT in El Salvador. Built to hold just over 1,300 high-security prisoners, mass transfers to the prison began in August 2025.

Argentina’s third-largest city, Rosario, has become an epicenter for drug trafficking and violence in the country in recent years. Less than ten miles away, construction for the High-Profile Inmate Detention Center (Centro de Reclusión para Internos de Alto Perfil – CERIAP), or “Hell” (“El Infierno”), as it has been nicknamed, is underway.

A Mega-Fixation on a Flawed Model

The term “megaprison” has become a buzzword for regional leaders attempting to signal a tough-on-crime stance. But so far, despite replicating Bukele’s playbook, none have achieved the same results.

While size alone does not account for CECOT’s success, most proposed facilities, despite being promoted as megaprisons, are considerably smaller.

But maximizing prison capacity is not a dependable recipe for success. 

History has shown that jailing large numbers of people is not an effective anti-crime policy. Understaffed and underfunded prisons are breeding grounds for violence. Inmates form groups for protection and begin to compete for turf and business within prison walls. Many of the region’s most powerful criminal groups were forged inside overcrowded prisons, including Tren de Aragua, which formed in Venezuela’s Tocorón prison and in a few short years became the regional bogeyman of organized crime; Brazil’s biggest criminal groups, the First Capital Command (Primeiro Comando da Capital – PCC) and Red Command (Comando Vermelho); as well as the Choneros, the Lobos, and the Tiguerones in Ecuador. In El Salvador, as well, prisons used to function as de facto headquarters for the gangs. Starting behind bars did little to curb these groups’ growth; most came to control the prisons they occupied, using them as spaces to coordinate criminal activities, a steady stream of recruits, and a springboard to expand onto the streets. 

SEE ALSO: The InSight Take: El Salvador’s Mass Trials Put Bukele’s Gang Crackdown on Display

CECOT is an exception because of its focus on imprisonment for life and its extremely restrictive conditions. Inmates are not allowed any contact with family or the outside world and are confined in crowded, windowless cells. They are mostly denied access to legal counsel and are subjected to solitary confinement for any alleged misbehavior. These conditions in themselves violate prisoners’ human rights, but there have also been reports of systematic physical and psychological abuse. In mass trials of hundreds of prisoners at a time, collective sentences of hundreds or even thousands of years are being passed. While this extreme subjugation has succeeded in subduing gangs in El Salvador, political opposition, civic resistance, and financial restrictions hinder other countries from replicating the model. 

What’s more, megaprisons address symptoms of organized crime rather than the causes. In Panama, poverty drives gang growth. In Costa Rica, drug traffickers have seized on port vulnerability to establish themselves. In Guatemala, rampant corruption undermines security efforts, allowing gangs to flourish. Surging production and trafficking of cocaine from Colombia and Peru and through Ecuador continue to drive criminal competition and growth in those countries and around the region. Megaprisons are, at best, a partial response to these problems rooted in deeper social, political, and economic conditions.

Sources and Methodology

This investigation is based on a review of government statements, official press releases, reports, and other publicly available sources. When media reports were used, information was verified across multiple independent outlets. Satellite imagery was also used to confirm the location, construction, and status of prison facilities where possible. 

*Amanda Rocha contributed to the research for this article.

The post Mapping Latin America’s Megaprisons appeared first on InSight Crime.

Brazil Crackdown Reveals New Tren de Aragua Playbook

A recent police operation in northern Brazil has revealed how the Venezuelan-born gang Tren de Aragua has established presence in the country and adapted its model of criminal expansion through alliances.

item.content:encoded:
Brazil Crackdown Reveals New Tren de Aragua Playbook

A recent police operation in northern Brazil has revealed how the Venezuelan-born gang Tren de Aragua has established a presence in the country and adapted its model of criminal expansion through alliances.

Police in the northern state of Roraima, which borders Venezuela, reportedly dismantled a branch of Tren de Aragua operating in Brazil in June. The cell allegedly used the state to traffic weapons to other parts of the country and partnered with local criminal groups to launder money from illegal mining, drug trafficking, and other illicit activities.  

Seizures also took place in Amazonas—another state in the north of Brazil—as well as in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, and Paraná in the southeastern and southern regions.

SEE ALSO: Tren de Aragua: Fact vs. Fiction

Officials captured 13 people and froze R$429 million (around $82 million) in bank accounts and financial assets linked to suspected members of the network. 

Evidence from the investigation suggests that Tren de Aragua worked with Brazil’s Red Command (Comando Vermelho – CV), Brazil’s second-largest gang, which was recently designated as a terrorist organization by the United States. 

This alliance represents a different method for the Venezuelan gang: instead of establishing itself as a dominant criminal power, as it has done in other countries, Tren de Aragua seems to be allying with local gangs in Brazil to extend its reach and profits.

Tren de Aragua in Brazil

The dismantling of the Tren de Aragua network in Brazil demonstrates how the group has made inroads there in recent years.

Tren de Aragua allegedly provided weapons acquired in the United States, Colombia, and Venezuela to Red Command members in Amazonas and Rio de Janeiro, often in exchange for cocaine, said Military Police Colonel Francisco Xavier. Tren de Aragua then sold the cocaine in Roraima, he told InSight Crime.

In other cases, weapons were paid in cash, so Tren de Aragua established a money laundering system using front companies to launder funds. According to Xavier, the group worked with the same network that set up front companies for the Red Command.

These collaborators operate as brokers, without ties to specific criminal organizations. “Whenever there’s a major [criminal] financial operator, they provide services to more than one client. They’re in the market and offer their service to whoever hires them,” Anchieta Nery, Director of Integrated Operations and Intelligence at the National Secretariat of Public Security (Secretaria Nacional de Segurança Pública – Senasp), told InSight Crime.

Tren de Aragua’s biggest presence in Brazil is in Roraima, which borders the state of Bolívar in southern Venezuela. Bolívar has long been a seat of power for Las Claritas Sindicato, a mining gang with deep ties to Tren de Aragua through its cofounder Yohan José Romero, alias “Johan Petrica.” The small town of Las Claritas, located in the Sifontes municipality, became Tren de Aragua’s sanctuary after a state intervention displaced the group from their headquarters in Tocorón prison in Aragua state in 2023. 

Roraima’s police say Tren de Aragua has been expanding in Brazil since 2018, capitalizing on waves of Venezuelan migrants moving into the country to establish a foothold in new territories. Tren de Aragua’s money laundering activities now extend to Brazil’s southern and southeastern states.

A New Modus Operandi

In other parts of Latin America, Tren de Aragua’s expansion model involved setting up cells and taking over local criminal economies by using extreme violence and exploiting Venezuelan migrants. But in Brazil, the group has taken a different approach. 

In the wave of migration that gathered pace in 2015, millions of Venezuelans left their home country, with the majority settling in Colombia, Chile, and Peru. Tren de Aragua followed them, initially making money off human smuggling and trafficking. In Chile and Peru, the group found illicit markets ready to be exploited, among them extortion, the sex trade, and retail sale of drugs, with little local competition, ill-prepared security forces, and large Venezuelan diasporas living on the legal margins, and thus ripe for exploitation.

At first, in Brazil, Tren de Aragua’s expansion seemed to follow a similar pattern, with its presence initially concentrated along the border, following migration routes. Roraima offered a financial hub to launder money, as well as smuggle goods and minerals mined in Venezuela, as other illegal mining groups did. 

But, unlike in Chile and Peru, where new Tren de Aragua cells quickly multiplied and spread, Tren de Aragua’s armed growth was limited—much like in Medellín, Colombia’s overcrowded underworld—by Brazil’s bigger and stronger organized crime actors, the Red Command and the PCC. Roraima is mainly under the control of the First Capital Command (Primeiro Comando da Capital – PCC), Brazil’s largest and most powerful criminal organization.

SEE ALSO: Tren de Aragua Clashes with Colombia’s Underworld

In Brazil, Tren de Aragua seems to have expanded as a service provider instead, using its alliance with the Red Command to establish networks that support and extend its activities in Brazil, without investing in armed cells or needing territorial control or monopoly over criminal markets.

“There is an identity symbiosis between Tren de Aragua and the Red Command; members of the Venezuelan gang even request to stay in the same prison wings as the Red Command,” Wesley Costa de Oliveira, a Roraima Civil Police chief in charge of the investigation, told InSight Crime.

The Red Command’s alliance with Tren de Aragua has helped both groups extend their reach. According to Xavier, the Red Command is growing stronger in the north thanks to the Venezuelan gang providing weapons and logistics. Data from a 2025 report by the Brazilian Forum of Public Security (Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública – FBSP) shows that the Red Command more than doubled its presence in the Amazon region since 2023.

“We are seeing members of the PCC ‘tearing the shirt’ [defecting] to join the Red Command. While the PCC is still the dominant power in Roraima, the Red Command is gaining significant ground and prestige due to Venezuelan support,” Xavier said.

The post Brazil Crackdown Reveals New Tren de Aragua Playbook appeared first on InSight Crime.

Reshuffled or Reformed? Venezuela’s Criminal Order After Maduro

The unprecedented arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January shook Venezuela’s power structures—both legal and illegal. We’ve been tracking the impacts of his arrest and the underworld power struggle that followed.

The post Reshuffled or Reformed? Venezuela’s Criminal Order After Maduro appeared first on InSight Crime.
item.content:encoded:
Reshuffled or Reformed? Venezuela’s Criminal Order After Maduro

The arrest of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife on January 3 was an unprecedented aggression by the United States.  

At the time, President Donald Trump called Maduro the “kingpin of a vast criminal network”—the Cartel of the Suns—and linked him to Tren de Aragua and the Sinaloa Cartel, which his government has labeled terrorist organizations. 

This post is part of our annual Summer InSights series. See the full series here.

Maduro ran what we call “a hybrid state,” in which governance and crime became indistinguishable. Criminal groups became armed proxies for the state, crushing opposition and enforcing control in exchange for impunity. Corruption buried into state institutions—often mischaracterized as the Cartel of the Suns—used government as a private revenue generator. 

But how has Maduro’s extraction impacted crime in Venezuela? 

Less than one might think. The hybrid state remains mostly intact, despite some shuffling at the top by interim President Delcy Rodríguez, who is trying to balance her regime’s interests with Trump’s. Rodríguez has cooperated with the US government against Tren de Aragua and sidelined some of Maduro’s inner circle. But it’s otherwise business as usual for corruption, drug trafficking, and illegal mining.

What’s the latest on the US case against Nicolás Maduro?

Brazil keeps targeting the PCC's finances—but is it working?

And what does the arrest of a former Mexican governor say about the country's fuel theft market?

This week's top three organized crime stories in On the Radar.

item.content:encoded:
On the Radar: Maduro Trial Takes Shape as Brazil Targets PCC Finances

What’s the latest on the US case against Nicolás Maduro?

Brazil keeps targeting the PCC’s finances—but is it working?

And what does the arrest of a former Mexican governor say about the country’s fuel theft market?

This week’s top three organized crime stories in On the Radar.

1. A Trial Date Takes Shape for Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores

Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein set the start of the narcoterrorism and drug trafficking trial against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, for June 2027. Maduro and Flores were arrested by US Special Forces at a safe house in Caracas during a January 3 raid and flown to New York to face charges.

The name Cartel of the Suns—the alleged network of corrupt officials in the Venezuelan government—has been used by prosecutors, both in the original 2020 indictment and in the Trump administration’s messaging ahead of Maduro’s capture. But the newer charges unsealed after his arrest barely mention the term, leaning instead on more general narco-terrorism and cocaine charges. 

2. São Paulo Prosecutors Target PCC Money Network

São Paulo launched “Operação Janus” this week against a group accused of laundering money for the First Capital Command (Primeiro Comando da Capital – PCC). Nearly 20 people were arrested and their properties searched. Authorities also froze some 10 million reais (about $1.8 million) in assets per suspect and imposed restrictions on companies allegedly tied to the scheme. 

Operação Janus, which also reportedly implicates senior police officials, is the latest hit to the PCC’s increasingly complex financial operations that have roped in sectors as diverse as the oil industry to influencers. The group was also recently designated a foreign terrorist group by the United States. 

3. Former Mexican Governor Arrested Over Fuel Theft

Mexican authorities arrested Ernesto Ruffo Appel—the ex-governor of Baja California—on organized crime and fuel theft charges. Ruffo has been put in pretrial detention. Ruffo’s arrest is the latest sign of how far huachicol fiscal—as tax-dodging fuel smuggling schemes are known in Mexico—has reached into the country’s political and business elite and continues to fuel violence there.

Visit InSightCrime.org for more on Venezuela news and profiles, ongoing coverage of the PCC, and Mexico’s fuel-theft economy.

item.content:encoded:
The Final Chapter for Tren de Aragua Founder Larry Changa?

Larry Amaury Álvarez Núñez, alias “Larry Changa,” is set to be tried on charges of criminal association and kidnapping in Chile after Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro greenlit his extradition. If convicted, it could be the final chapter in the criminal history of one of the three founding members of Tren de Aragua, Venezuela’s most infamous criminal export.

Changa, who was born in Maracay, Aragua state, in May 1977, started off stealing vehicles and auto parts across Aragua and the neighboring state of Carabobo in the late 1990s and was arrested for car theft in 2002. A conviction for homicide and aggravated robbery followed, landing him in Tocorón prison.

SEE ALSO: Larry Amaury Álvarez Núñez, alias “Larry Changa.”

Inside Tocorón, Álvarez fell in with two other inmates, Héctor “Niño Guerrero” Guerrero and Yohan “Johan Petrica” Romero. Together, the trio ran Tren de Aragua from behind bars, turning Tocorón into a gang-governed criminal fiefdom complete with a zoo and nightclub while extending the gang’s reach outside the prison walls, building a vast criminal enterprise involved in extortion, human trafficking, and smuggling.

SEE ALSO: Tren de Aragua: Fact or Fiction?

In 2015, Changa escaped Tocorón and vanished from view until resurfacing in Chile in 2018, where he spent the next several years building Tren de Aragua’s first Chilean faction. Changa allegedly led a structure—including a cell known as “the Piratas de Aragua”—that Chilean investigators say extorted, kidnapped, and murdered while laundering criminal proceeds through a network of businesses. 

Changa fled Chile in 2022. Despite being the subject of an Interpol red notice active in 196 countries, he remained free until Colombian police arrested him while driving a luxury vehicle in Circasia, a municipality in the department of Quindío in the heart of Colombia’s coffee district.
